Continual fine-tuning without regularization asks: as a transformer is sequentially adapted to new tasks, do attention heads progressively collapse toward functional equivalence — and if so, does this collapse accelerate, stabilize, or interact destructively with task-specific representations already encoded? The key concepts are attention head redundancy (measurable via cosine similarity of attention weight matrices or centered kernel alignment of head outputs), continual learning's catastrophic forgetting, and the distinction between parameter redundancy and functional redundancy — a subtlety beginners collapse too quickly. Experts worry about something beginners miss entirely: redundancy is not uniform across layers. Early layers, which tend to encode positional and syntactic patterns, may tolerate head collapse better than middle-to-late layers where task-specific compositional representations live, meaning aggregate redundancy metrics can look benign while the model is quietly hemorrhaging capacity in the layers that matter. A second expert concern is that redundancy accumulation is not monotonic — fine-tuning on a new task can transiently decrease redundancy as new gradients diversify heads, followed by re-collapse, creating a deceptive signal if you only checkpoint at task boundaries. The practical danger is that by task three or four, you may have exhausted the effective head budget in critical layers without any single fine-tuning step having produced an alarming loss spike.

The sharpest metric for functional redundancy is agreement on which tokens get attended to across inputs — concretely, measuring the average Jensen-Shannon divergence between two heads' attention distributions over a held-out corpus, rather than comparing W_Q, W_K, W_V matrices directly. Michel et al. (2019, "Are Sixteen Heads Really Better than One?") showed that heads with nearly identical weight-space signatures can produce divergent attention patterns on out-of-distribution inputs, meaning weight cosine similarity systematically understates true functional diversity under distribution shift — exactly the regime continual fine-tuning creates. A more demanding functional metric is Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) on head output vectors (the post-softmax weighted value sums), which Nguyen et al. and subsequent BERT probing work found stabilizes around 0.85–0.95 between redundant heads on in-distribution data but drops sharply when the input domain shifts. The metric choice changes your collapse timeline materially: weight-space similarity often shows apparent convergence after the first fine-tuning task, while output-CKA and attention-JSD metrics may not signal functional redundancy until task two or three, because early fine-tuning shifts weights without yet aligning the functional routing behavior those weights produce. Practically, if you use weight similarity as your early-warning signal, you'll conclude redundancy is already severe before task-specific heads have actually lost their discriminative behavior — triggering premature pruning or regularization that discards still-functional capacity. The operationally honest approach is to run both: weight similarity as a cheap proxy for potential redundancy, and output-CKA on a diverse probe set as the confirmation gate before any intervention.

The most trustworthy online signal is the effective rank of the cross-task activation alignment matrix — concretely, computing CKA between the current batch's layer activations and a compressed summary (e.g., a reservoir sample) of prior-task activations at the same layer, updated every N steps, with a threshold drop (say, CKA falling below 0.3 in two or more consecutive middle layers) triggering a regime-change flag. This is preferable to loss-based signals because loss can stay low during the early phase of a distribution-shift fine-tuning run if the new task is superficially similar in output space but representationally distant — the model fits the new task by overwriting middle-layer geometry while output-layer statistics remain stable, meaning perplexity or task loss gives you no warning until the damage is done. The late-firing problem is real and severe: because transformer fine-tuning updates propagate through the network with a delay — early layers adapt more slowly than late layers under standard learning rate schedules — the diversity basis in middle layers can be substantially overwritten within the first 50–200 steps of a new task before your CKA-based detector, which needs enough new-task batches to stabilize its estimate, has accumulated sufficient signal to fire. Frankston and colleagues' work on representation drift in sequential fine-tuning (and related observations in the LoRA continual learning literature) suggest that the first 5–10% of fine-tuning steps on a new task account for a disproportionate fraction of representational change — meaning the detection window and the damage window are nearly co-incident, leaving almost no reaction time. A partial mitigation is to front-load detection by using a probing classifier trained on prior-task activations: if a lightweight linear probe's accuracy on held-out prior-task data drops more than 15% within the first 20 steps, that's a faster signal than CKA stabilization requires, though it demands maintaining prior-task probe data online. The irreversibility question hinges on whether the overwritten diversity basis can be reconstructed from the remaining heads and the prior-task data reservoir — and for highly over-parameterized models this may be possible via targeted re-diversification, but for models operating near their effective head-capacity limit in critical layers, the answer is likely no: once two heads have collapsed to the same functional attractor in a low-capacity layer, there is no gradient signal from prior-task data alone that can re-separate them without reintroducing the new-task loss conflict you were trying to avoid.

The systematic misleading case is distributional mode collapse in the probe: if your 100–500 sample probe is drawn from the most common or most easily available examples of the new task (which is typical in practice — you grab the first N examples), it will oversample high-frequency input patterns and undersample the rare compositional structures that actually drive the largest gradient updates during full fine-tuning, causing you to protect subspace directions activated by common inputs while leaving unprotected exactly the directions that rare but high-gradient examples will hit hardest. The practical consequence is that your anticipatory constraint becomes asymmetrically protective — it successfully shields prior-task diversity from the common new-task inputs but provides no protection against the tail of the new-task distribution, which may be responsible for 30–50% of total representational drift based on analogous findings in curriculum learning literature.
